Drakkar · curation report

Checking the AI curation

Whether the short viral mappings Claude recorded hold up against their publications, and whether it finds as many of them as curation by hand.

By Claude, for the Drakkar curation team · 16 November 2026 · from the live vh descriptions of Drakkar on that day, read-only, and the full texts the AI curation worked from

99 / 99distinct short viral mappings of the AI curation found in their publication, correctly placed
5.4 %of the AI's publications have a short viral mapping, against 5.7 % by hand, on the same literature
92of the AI's 99 distinct short viral sequences new to Drakkar
652publications curated by the AI, with 50,864 live descriptions

In short

  • The AI's short viral mappings are right. All 99 distinct sequences of 5 to 20 residues are in their publication: 62 written in its files, 32 placed exactly where the coordinates of their note put them, 5 printed in a figure. None is ambiguously placed; one reaches 94 % identity, a strain difference its note states.
  • On the same literature, the AI finds as many. In runs 81 and 85, the only runs curated partly by hand and partly by the AI, a publication has a short viral mapping as often under both curations: 5.4 % of the AI's, 5.7 % of the manual ones, and 5.6 % against 5.7 % without the screens, which only the AI curated. It has a viral mapping at all a little more often under the AI: 41 % against 34 %.
  • Across the whole curation, the rates are of the same order. The AI curation holds 99 distinct short viral sequences in 652 publications, 15 per 100 publications; the manual curation 1,354 in 6,019, 22 per 100. On both sides a few peptide screens carry most of them. 92 of the AI's 99 were not yet in Drakkar.
  • The AI records a little more per publication: median 4 descriptions against 2 in runs 81 and 85, one per experiment and strain tested, as the rules ask. Its far larger totals come from screens, which the manual curation of runs 81 and 85 left out: there, 24 AI publications of more than 100 descriptions hold 12,552 of its 13,889 descriptions.
  • Its longer mappings and lower identities come from UniProt. It curated on UniProt 2026, whose viral section shrank from 4.91 to 1.11 million entries: a strain that had its own entry now often has none, and its construct is recorded on the closest entry.

How the analysis was done

Data

Everything counted comes from the live vh descriptions of Drakkar on 16 November 2026, read on a read-only connection: nothing was written. The unit of comparison is the publication with at least one live vh description; a publication curated with no description has nothing to compare and is left out. A publication is AI-curated when its last curation pass was the AI's, otherwise manual.

Years: the publication years of the middle 80 % of the group. The main comparison is runs 81 and 85: their publications, from the same PubMed weeks, were shared out between the two curations, which there face the same literature, except the screens, which the manual curation left out and the AI curation took. Recent manual and all manual give context: their publications differ from the AI's in years and topics. Every table and chart below can switch between the three comparisons.

Units

  • A mapping is one recorded sequence on the viral side of one description (the human side is left out): a peptide recorded on 944 descriptions is 944 mappings. A distinct sequence is a recorded sequence counted once, in a group or in a publication.
  • A mapping's length is the length of the recorded sequence, its extra end residues (an initiator methionine, a tag) included. Short means 5 to 20 residues.
  • Totals and means are driven by a few large screens, so the comparison relies on medians and distributions per publication, and every table can leave out the largest publications of each group.

Checks of the short viral mappings

Each distinct short viral sequence of the AI curation was checked against its publication, from the full texts the AI curation downloaded (article, supplementary files, all converted to text, kept for every AI publication). The publication is the reference: the database says what was recorded, only the publication says whether it is right. Each sequence gets a source:

  • Written: the sequence, as recorded or without its extra end residues, is written in one of the publication's text files: plain, residue by residue with spaces or hyphens, or in three-letter codes.
  • Coordinates: not written, but the description note gives a residue range (43-61, G378…D386) that is exactly where the mapping is placed on its protein, counted on the whole protein or on the mature protein.
  • Figure: printed only in an image; read by eye.

Then its placement, from the occurrences stored with the mapping: an identity below 100 %; several placements on the interactor (an ambiguous peptide); an exact match on the protein outside the interactor (a peptide that may belong to another mature protein); found only on an isoform; as long as the interactor itself; recorded on several viral interactors in one publication.

What it leaves to the review

Whether a mapping is missing is not checked here. Each AI publication was curated by one model, then reviewed against its full text by another, whose first target is what the curation misses, and every finding of the review was checked again before the commit. Recomputing that from the files would only be a weaker copy of it.

What it does not do

It never says which side is right where AI and manual curation differ: a difference is a question, not an error. The manual descriptions cannot be checked against their publications here: their full texts are not on disk. Nothing was read by hand except the figure behind five peptides and one match that looked suspicious (a 5-residue peptide found in a sentence about its mutation: the recorded peptide is the one the fluorescence polarization assay used).

Results

  none

Short viral mappings

The AI curation holds 1,134 short viral mappings on 1,077 descriptions, but only 99 distinct sequences, from 25 publications. 37659653 alone accounts for 944 mappings: one HPV16 E7 peptide, recorded on each human partner of a peptide pull-down screen. 38698856, a peptide array of overlapping 20-mers of influenza HA, gives 37 distinct sequences, and the 24 other publications 62.

On the same literature, the AI finds them as often. In runs 81 and 85, 12 of the 222 AI publications (5.4 %) have a short viral mapping, against 7 of the 123 manual ones (5.7 %); without the screens, which only the AI curated, 5.6 % against 5.7 %. On each side, one publication holds most of the distinct sequences: 38473724 gives 75 of the manual side's 84, the HA peptide array 38698856 37 of the AI side's 57; without them, the other 6 manual publications hold 9 and the other 11 AI publications 20.

Across the whole curation, the rates are of the same order. The AI curation holds 15 distinct short sequences per 100 publications, the manual curation 22 (1,354 in 6,019 publications), over two decades of literature and its peptide screens. Against the recent manual group the gap is wider: 3.8 % of the AI publications have a short viral mapping, against 6.0 % of the recent manual ones, whose 405 distinct sequences come for 335 from two publications, a phage-display screen (37100772) and 38473724.

92 of the AI's 99 distinct short sequences are new to Drakkar: only 7 had already been recorded by the manual curation.

As to placement: 1 below 100 % identity (a strain difference stated in its note), 0 with several placements on its interactor, 0 found on the protein outside its interactor, 0 found only on an isoform, 0 as long as its interactor, 0 recorded on several viral interactors of one publication. No sequence is shared by two AI publications.

Publications

In runs 81 and 85, the AI side holds 13,889 descriptions and the manual side 689. Almost all of the gap is screens: 24 AI publications of more than 100 descriptions each (proximity labelling, affinity purification, peptide pull-downs) hold 12,552 of the AI's descriptions, against 1 such manual publication with 158. The other publications compare at a human scale: 198 AI publications with 1,337 descriptions, median 3 each, against 122 manual ones with 531, median 2. The gap is in which publications each side took, not in how deeply it curated them: the manual curation of these runs left out the screens, which no one could then load by script, and the AI curation curated them like any other publication. Earlier runs did get their screens loaded by script, which is why the recent and all manual groups have large publications too.

The AI does record a little more per publication, as the rules ask: one description per experiment and per strain tested, supplementary panels included, which the benchmark on run 74 showed too. Over all the publications of runs 81 and 85, it records a median of 4 descriptions against 2, with 2 human interactors against 1. Over the whole AI curation, screens drive the totals as well: 40593736, a SARS-CoV-2 interactome of run 82, holds 11,722 of the AI's 50,864 descriptions (23 %). Move the slider to leave out the largest publications of each group: the totals and means fall, the medians stay put.

What is curated

The share of publications using each method, and studying each virus family. The AI names the assay as performed: in runs 81 and 85 as well as against the recent manual group, it uses anti bait coimmunoprecipitation more and the generic coimmunoprecipitation less. The virus families are close in runs 81 and 85; against the recent manual group, whose publications come from the 2022–2023 peak of SARS-CoV-2 work, coronaviruses weigh less.

Mappings

In runs 81 and 85, a publication gets a viral mapping a little more often from the AI: 41 % of the AI publications against 34 % of the manual ones. Across the other groups the shares are close: 38 % of all AI publications, 40 % of the recent manual ones. Counted per description, the AI's share looks lower against the recent manual group, 7.3 % against 15.6 %, only because its large screens add thousands of descriptions without a mapping.

The AI's viral mappings are longer. Part of it is repetition: a screen run with a fragment of a viral protein as bait carries that fragment on every hit, so 40872852 repeats one fragment of EBV BPLF1 on 965 descriptions and 38898526 one fragment of Gag on 436. Counting each sequence once per publication, the AI still leans long: its 575 distinct viral sequences have a median length of 149 residues against 44 in the whole manual curation, 232 of them over 200 residues: domains and deletion constructs, recorded as the construct the experiment used.

Long mappings and strains

The two curations did not choose their entries in the same UniProt. The manual curation worked on UniProt 2021_02, whose viral section held 4.91 million entries: 4,893,260 unreviewed (TrEMBL) and 17,014 reviewed (Swiss-Prot), many of them single strains and isolates. In June 2025, UniProt announced that UniProtKB would keep only the sequences of reference proteomes, besides Swiss-Prot and entries with important extra data such as a 3D structure, and that its viral reference proteomes would follow the exemplar genomes of the ICTV; the restriction came with release 2026_02. Release 2026_03, which Drakkar now uses and the AI curation worked on, holds 1.11 million viral entries: 1,092,202 unreviewed and 17,529 reviewed. The reviewed section barely changed: what went is the nearly four million unreviewed entries outside the reference proteomes. A strain that had its own entry when the manual curation chose it now often has none, and the rules then assign the closest entry by sequence.

Does this make the AI's long viral mappings strains recorded on a reference entry? Few are. Of the AI's 232 distinct viral sequences over 200 residues (each counted once per publication), 27 cover 95 % or more of their interactor, 15 of them below 100 % identity: a strain without an entry, recorded on the closest one (an H9N2 HA at 97.4 %, for instance); the others are constructs without a signal peptide or a tail. 154 cover less than 80 %: fragments, domains and deletion constructs. The strain effect shows in identity instead: 84 of the AI's 575 distinct viral sequences are below 100 % identity, against 5 of 688 in the recent manual curation. With fewer strain entries in UniProt, more constructs come from a strain other than their entry's, and the rules keep their own residues rather than adapting them to the entry.

Sources: Drakkar, live vh descriptions on 16 November 2026 (read-only); the full texts of the AI curation's runs, as downloaded for it. The groups, units and checks are those described above; the data behind every table is embedded in this page.
